desc:
Some squares of an n × n board are blocked: blocked[i] = [row, col] (0-based). A queen may not be placed on a blocked square. Blocked squares do not stop queens from attacking through them.

Count the ways to place n queens on the board, none of them on a blocked square, so that no two queens share a row, a column or a diagonal.

n = 4, blocked = []              →  2
n = 4, blocked = [[0,1]]         →  1
n = 4, blocked = [[0,1],[0,2]]   →  0
constraints: All blocked squares are distinct and inside the board
hints: Exactly one queen goes into each row, so search row by row and count the complete placements.
Track which columns and which two kinds of diagonals are already attacked. For row r a column c is usable only if it is not attacked and (r, c) is not blocked.
Store the blocked cells of every row as a bitmask. The set of usable columns in a row is then full & ~(cols | diag1 | diag2 | blockedMask[r]), and you can iterate its set bits.
editorial: This is the classic N-Queens count with one extra restriction. Search row by row. In row r the candidate columns are those that are not in a used column, not on an attacked diagonal and not blocked in this row. For every candidate place the queen, recurse into the next row and add the returned counts.

Bitmasks make the candidate computation a few machine operations: keep a mask of used columns, a mask of attacked columns on the down-left diagonals (shift left by one when moving to the next row) and one for the down-right diagonals (shift right). The blocked cells of each row form one more mask that is OR-ed in. Blocking only removes candidates; it never changes how attacks propagate. For n = 10 the unblocked board has 724 solutions and a few ten thousand search nodes, so the search is instant.
